name: Olga Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, political parties or government, and your answers are confidential. What does your workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Olga Young, 43, and I work as a junior hand on building sites. I left school before finishing and I'm still learning the trade, so I cut backing pieces, fix boards and help with door frames while the lead checks my work. I enjoy seeing a damp, bare room become usable; I dislike finding out a pipe was in the wall after the board is already on. I have learned to ask before drilling.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What are you balancing at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Tariq does night shifts in a care home, and our children are eleven and sixteen. We have a mortgage and about two months of expenses saved, with my construction pay about normal for the job. There are some other builders nearby, but I wouldn't count on walking straight into one. I use AI now and then to sort a parts list, after a coworker shows me it works; I don't let it choose a place to drill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that a tidy parts list saves walking up and down stairs, but the pipe finder still decides where I drill. If the office likes AI for forms, I don't mind as long as the site gets what it ordered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my site work and pay stay about the same. Two months of savings sounds comfortable until a contract pauses. My partner Tariq's night hours cannot carry the whole mortgage and both children's needs for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my paid shifts and use a tested AI parts list only for simple rooms. In the first year I'd compare its count with my paper sketch before ordering, and I'd keep asking the lead to check my door-frame measurements.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. The technology doesn't threaten my own wage here, but a stopped project would use up two months quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why only simple rooms?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A square room with two doors is easy to count twice. An old room with three odd corners has fooled people who know far more than the phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a paused contract mean at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We could skip a family weekend away and stay current on the mortgage for a while. I wouldn't tell the children everything was fine if we were living out of savings.

say: I would accept **parts-list help** while keeping a pipe finder at the drill.
I would ask the office to deliver the **right materials**.
think: My **site wage** should continue under modest AI change.
A stopped contract could eat **two months** of savings quickly.
do: Keep **paid shifts** and have frame measurements checked.
Compare an **AI parts count** with a paper sketch on simple rooms.
feel: **Uneasy** about paused construction work and the mortgage.
S0.quote: Two months of savings sounds comfortable until a contract pauses.
fieldNote: Olga accepts a **tested narrow tool**, while her pipe-finding habit shows why she keeps final decisions on site.
A **two-month reserve** and mortgage leave her alert to ordinary project gaps even when AI barely changes the job.

steps.text: Keep paid site shifts and ask lead to check door-frame measurements
Compare AI parts count against paper sketch on simple rooms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the manager to test the new buying system against actual deliveries for a month before setting crew targets from it. A software promise is not a box of hinges on the floor where we need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Faster planning may help, but it might also let the builder promise tighter jobs and then send a junior home when the numbers don't add up. My hours could shrink; Tariq's care-home wage would cover basics for a short time, not all our mortgage and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working my shifts and ask the lead to show me how the new ordering screen works after it has been tried by another crew. In the first year I'd log missing materials and hours lost, then ask the manager whether we can train on wet-room repairs during paid time; I'd look at other site openings if our rota falls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can learn a screen, but I cannot pay the mortgage with time saved by somebody else's buying software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wet-room repairs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We had a bathroom job where the waterproof layer failed, and the repair crew spent two days putting it right. I want to learn the sealing properly, but I wouldn't sell myself as a repairer after watching one job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would convince you about the ordering screen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three jobs where the right items arrive on the right day. Then I'd use it, provided someone still answers when the list and the site disagree.

say: I would ask for a **month’s trial** before buying software sets targets.
I would point out that software cannot replace **hinges on site**.
think: My **junior hours** could shrink under tighter bids.
Tariq’s **care-home wage** cannot carry all our costs for long.
do: Learn the **ordering screen** after another crew tests it.
Log **missing materials** and request paid wet-room repair training.
Check **other site openings** if the rota falls.
feel: **Anxious** about losing hours through tighter planning.
S1.quote: I cannot pay the mortgage with time saved by somebody else's buying software.
fieldNote: She asks for **three working jobs** before trusting a new screen, matching her measured approach to change.
Her own **junior rota** could fall, so she combines logged evidence, paid learning and conditional job searches.

steps.text: Learn ordering screen after another crew tests it on site
Request paid wet-room repair training after logging material delays
Check other builder openings if current rota falls
Keep paid site shifts while evaluating new buying system

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my children that AGI can do the plans by 2028, and robots able to do site work come around 2031. I'd also tell them we are checking what work remains, not packing the house tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm still learning, so AGI might take the simple ordering work I have just learned to do. The physical jobs may last three more years, but by 2031 I expect my site hours to fall sharply when robots can cut and fix as well as people. Two months saved is not enough to carry a mortgage through that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd ask a local training centre about a paid placement in building maintenance, with real hours attached, and apply if a place exists. In 2029 I'd keep taking site shifts and use AGI parts lists only after a lead checks them; at the first cut in hours Tariq and I would talk to the lender.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can try a different job, but there is not enough cash to make two years of wrong turns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is building maintenance safe from robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The reports may go to AGI in 2028, and the physical repairs can follow when robots arrive. I want a paid way to keep working during the change, not a promise of permanent safety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Tariq add more night shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tariq could ask, but the care home does not always have them and night work has a cost at home. I would not put all four of us on a plan that depends on unlimited extra shifts.

say: I would explain **2028 AGI** before **2031 robots** to the children.
I would say we are checking paid options before making **housing decisions**.
think: My **ordering task** may disappear under AGI.
My **site hours** could fall sharply when capable robots reach physical work.
do: Apply for a **paid maintenance placement** if one exists.
Keep **site shifts** and check AGI parts lists in 2029.
Contact the **lender** with Tariq as soon as site hours fall.
feel: **Alarmed** by a likely wage shock beyond two months saved.
S2.quote: I can try a different job, but there is not enough cash to make two years of wrong turns.
fieldNote: She expects **planning tasks** to change in 2028, followed by a deeper site-wage shock when robots arrive.
The household has only **two months saved**, so she asks for paid placement and lender help before considering a move.

steps.text: Apply to local centre for paid building-maintenance placement if available
Keep taking paid construction shifts in 2029
Check AGI parts lists with site lead before orders in 2029
Talk to mortgage lender with Tariq at first cut in hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew five years gives us time to test repair training on real jobs before deciding whether to leave building sites. AGI arrives for plans in 2031, while robots arrive for fitting about 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 I may still earn by fitting boards, though AGI could cut a few ordering hours. At 51 in 2034, capable robots might take the simple site tasks that keep a junior worker paid; I expect fewer shifts unless I have proved I can handle another role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the lead this year for paid time learning waterproofing on one bathroom repair, and I'd write down every step I can do correctly. By 2032 I'd apply for a maintenance helper opening if my record is good; in the first year after 2031 I'd use AI work orders only after a coworker shows me a reliable version.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with more room to practise than in the quick version. Five years helps me build evidence, but it doesn't promise the maintenance vacancy will exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make your repair record good?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two bathrooms where the lead signs off the sealed joints and no leak comes back after testing. One observation would not be enough for me to ask another employer to trust my work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for your own course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could pay a small fee if it came with a real placement, but I would not empty the reserve for a certificate alone. We need that money for the mortgage if the builder has a gap.

say: I would use the **five years** to test paid repair skills.
I would tell coworkers **2031 plans** and **2034 fitting** change at different times.
think: My **ordering hours** may fall after AGI arrives.
My **junior shifts** could shrink sharply when robots handle simple fitting.
do: Learn **waterproofing** on a paid bathroom repair and record sign-offs.
Apply for a **maintenance helper** opening by 2032 if qualified.
Use **AI work orders** only after a proven demonstration.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to practise but no guaranteed vacancy.
S3.quote: Five years helps me build evidence, but it doesn't promise the maintenance vacancy will exist.
fieldNote: Her **waterproofing test** requires two signed-off bathrooms, a concrete standard for moving toward maintenance.
She accepts **proven AI work orders** and a small course fee only with a placement, protecting mortgage savings.

steps.text: Learn waterproofing on paid bathroom repair with lead sign-off
Apply for maintenance helper post by 2032 if record qualifies
Use AI work orders after coworker demonstrates reliable version
Keep paid site shifts while building repair record

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my children that they'll be grown before the robots reach our site, but Tariq and I will still need to earn. I'll be 53 at AGI in 2036 and 56 when hands-on robots come around 2039, not ready to stop working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 our older child will be twenty-six and the younger twenty-one; school lunches and uniforms should not be the same bill, though we may help them start out. The mortgage may be smaller, but I cannot assume a pension or a safe site job once robots can do the fitting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep paid construction work now and put a modest amount from each full month into our reserve. Over the next two years I'd take paid wet-room repairs with the lead if available; in 2037 I'd apply for maintenance posts and use proven AGI ordering tools while comparing the wages to what I still earn on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than frightened today. Ten years gives me time to prove a repair skill, but it doesn't turn age 56 into a paid retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask the older child to help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if they choose to and live with us; at twenty-six they may have their own bills. We cannot make our mortgage depend on that possibility.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if wet-room work also becomes robotic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I would look at which paid maintenance tasks remain and whether I can do them. I would not buy tools for a private repair business until I had real customers and a clear price.

say: I would tell my children that **grown children** do not replace wages.
I would remind the crew I still need work at **56**.
think: Today’s **school costs** will change as the children become adults.
Neither a **pension** nor a safe site role is guaranteed after robots.
do: Keep **paid building work** and add modest monthly savings.
Take **paid wet-room repairs** with the lead if offered.
Apply for **maintenance posts** in 2037 and test proven AGI tools.
feel: **Uneasy** about wages after 2039, with time to prepare.
S4.quote: Ten years gives me time to prove a repair skill, but it doesn't turn age 56 into a paid retirement.
fieldNote: She correctly ages both children and treats **adult costs** as different, without counting on their income.
Her **longer runway** supports monthly saving and proven repair work, while she still expects robot pressure on site wages.

steps.text: Keep earning paid construction shifts through the decade
Add modest amount to reserve after each full-pay month
Take paid wet-room repair shifts with lead if offered
Apply for maintenance posts in 2037 if record qualifies

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most because my work might be cut before I've learned another job, and the robots follow in 2031. A paid maintenance placement, clear notice about hours and a lender who speaks to us early would help. We have a reserve, but it isn't large enough to live on while I guess my way into a new trade.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether the training is tested on real rooms. I would trust a course more if a lead watched me seal a bathroom and checked it after the water test. A certificate without that would not make me confident enough to take someone's home apart.

headlineQuote: A certificate without that would not make me confident enough to take someone's home apart.
portrait: Olga is a **43-year-old junior** site worker learning carpentry after leaving school early.
A **mortgage**, two school-age children and two months saved make wage gaps serious.
She uses **AI occasionally** after coworkers demonstrate it, and checks lists against paper and physical measurements.
She seeks **paid waterproofing experience** and a maintenance opening before robots threaten simple fitting work.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** threatens her wage before she can prove another skill, with robots reaching site tasks by 2031.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid placement**, clear hours notice and early lender contact would help the household withstand lost shifts.
